flawed_step: Step 3: Given A, B disjoint and closed in subspace Y, one would need their closures in X to be disjoint so as to apply normality of X and intersect with Y. Only cl_X(A)∩Y=A and cl_X(B)∩Y=B are known; the closures may meet at points of X outside Y (works only when Y is closed).
counterexample: Tychonoff plank: X=[0,ω1]×[0,ω] is compact Hausdorff hence normal; Y=X\{(ω1,ω)} is not normal: A={(ω1,n):n<ω} and B={(α,ω):α<ω1} are disjoint closed in Y, but any open U⊇A contains (α,ω1]×{n} for all n with α<ω1 (countable sup), and any open V⊇B contains a neighbourhood of (α+1,ω) meeting (α,ω1]×{n}.
assessment_summary: T1 passes to subspaces, but separating disjoint closed sets does not: the proof breaks where one needs disjoint closures in X. The deleted Tychonoff plank is a non-normal subspace of a compact Hausdorff (normal) space, so the statement is false.
